title: OpenAI’s chief scientist has thoughts on how to limit AI development
content:
A new blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity.
Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.”
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.”
But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name) could be that measurement.
In Pachochki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.”
Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5.
“GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.”
So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.”

report.summary: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposes using perplexity, a next-token prediction metric, as a shared yardstick for setting industry-wide limits on frontier AI development.
report.background: For years the AI safety debate focused on what models can do, via benchmarks like MMLU, GPQA and SWE-bench. Those capability tests saturate quickly, so they are poor speedometers for a fast-moving frontier. The political context sharpened in 2025-2026: a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher accused labs of "gambling with our lives," Anthropic's IPO filing warned of "catastrophic or existential risks," and CEO Dario Amodei published a "pace the frontier" plan calling for common safety standards and limits on unchecked progress — a plan Sam Altman and Elon Musk appeared to endorse. That shifted the question from whether to slow down to how to measure speed. Pachocki's post, which Altman called "the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while," is an attempt to supply that missing instrument.
key_points: Perplexity, not a capability benchmark, is the proposed yardstick. It measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower is better. Pachocki argues capability benchmarks go stale fast as models improve, while perplexity has stayed "informative" across generations.

The post includes a chart of falling perplexity since GPT-3.5. GPT-4 sat at roughly 0.91 and was good at chain-of-thought reasoning; below 0.8, Pachocki says, "transformative capabilities" appeared in cybersecurity and mathematics — a claimed link between a loss number and real-world risk.

The mechanism is a threshold pledge: companies would agree not to push perplexity past a set level until their ability to understand and monitor AI behavior hits a concrete milestone. That is a capability-gated pause rather than a cap on compute or training runs.

It is a direct follow-on to Amodei's "pace the frontier" proposal, and the endorsement from Altman signals OpenAI wants to shape the measurement rather than resist the limits. Whoever defines the metric effectively writes the rules.

The obvious weakness: perplexity depends on tokenizer, dataset and architecture, making it hard to compare across labs, and it says little about agentic or reasoning ability. A single private loss curve is also unverifiable without third-party audit.
report.impact: If adopted, this would be the industry's first de facto speed limit, and the first serious attempt to move AI governance from principles to metrology. The upside is a simple, cheap, continuous signal that could trigger scrutiny before dangerous capabilities ship. The risk is Goodhart's law: labs optimize what is measured, and perplexity is a proxy for capability, not capability itself. Cross-lab comparability is unresolved — different tokenizers produce different numbers — so adoption would require an audited, standardized evaluation protocol, probably run by a neutral body. For developers, expect more published loss curves, new eval tooling, and possible gating of flagship releases. For users, slower flagship launches and more safety-monitoring features, but also more transparent, comparable reporting on how capable each generation actually is.
report.tools: To follow along, look at EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness and Stanford's HELM for standardized benchmarking, the UK AI Safety Institute's Inspect framework for safety evaluations, and METR's task suites for dangerous-capability testing. Hugging Face's evaluate library and transformers ship ready-made perplexity computation if you want to reproduce the metric on open models, and Epoch AI's benchmarking database tracks how frontier scores move over time.
